matcher: ています|ていました|ている|ていた
explanation: Attaches to a verb's て-form to describe an action in progress ("is doing") or, for many verbs, the resulting state after a change ("is/has become"). Which meaning applies depends on the verb itself, not the grammar point.

examples.japanese: 今、本を読んでいます。
examples.english: I am reading a book right now.

examples.japanese: 彼はもう帰っている。
examples.english: He has already gone home (and is home now).

matcher: たいです|たかった|たい
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem (ます-form minus ます) to express the speaker's own desire to do something: "want to ~". Describing someone else's desire this way usually needs an extra marker (～たがっている) instead.

examples.japanese: 日本語を勉強したいです。
examples.english: I want to study Japanese.

examples.japanese: 疲れたので、早く寝たかった。
examples.english: I was tired, so I wanted to go to sleep early.

matcher: なければなりません|なければならない|なきゃいけない|なきゃならない
explanation: A negative conditional ("if [one] doesn't ~") combined with "won't do/won't become", together meaning "must ~" / "have to ~". ～なきゃ is the common casual-speech contraction.

examples.japanese: 明日までにレポートを書かなければなりません。
examples.english: I have to write the report by tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 薬を飲まなきゃいけない。
examples.english: I have to take my medicine.

matcher: ことができます|ことができました|ことができる|ことができない
explanation: Attaches to a verb's dictionary form plus こと (nominalizing it: "the act of ~ing") plus できる ("is possible"), giving "can ~" / "is able to ~". More formal-sounding than a verb's own potential form (食べられる vs. 食べることができる).

examples.japanese: 彼女はピアノを弾くことができます。
examples.english: She can play the piano.

examples.japanese: この漢字を読むことができない。
examples.english: I can't read this kanji.

matcher: てもいいです|てもいいですか|てもいい
explanation: て-form plus も ("even") plus いい ("good"), literally "even if [one does], it's fine" -- used to grant or ask for permission: "may ~" / "it's okay to ~".

examples.japanese: ここに座ってもいいですか。
examples.english: Is it okay if I sit here?

examples.japanese: 写真を撮ってもいい。
examples.english: It's fine to take photos.

matcher: てはいけません|てはいけない|ちゃいけない|じゃいけない
explanation: て-form plus は (topic-marking the action) plus いけない ("no good/not allowed") -- the negative counterpart of ～てもいい: "must not ~" / "not allowed to ~". ～ちゃ/～じゃ are the common casual contractions of ～ては/～では.

examples.japanese: ここで走ってはいけません。
examples.english: You must not run here.

examples.japanese: 夜遅くまで遊んじゃいけないよ。
examples.english: You're not allowed to play out until late at night.

matcher: らしいです|らしかった|らしい
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form verb, adjective, or noun to mark information the speaker heard or inferred secondhand rather than knows firsthand: "apparently ~" / "I heard ~".

examples.japanese: 明日は雨らしいです。
examples.english: Apparently it's going to rain tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 隣の店はもう閉店したらしい。
examples.english: I heard the shop next door has already closed for good.

matcher: ようになりました|ようになる|ようになった
explanation: Attaches to a verb's dictionary or potential form plus よう ("way/manner") plus なる ("become"), describing a gradual change reaching a new state -- often "came to be able to ~" when following a potential-form verb.

examples.japanese: 毎日練習して、上手に泳げるようになりました。
examples.english: I practiced every day, and I became able to swim well.

examples.japanese: 最近、野菜を食べるようになった。
examples.english: Recently, I've started eating vegetables (I didn't used to).

matcher: すれば|なれば|あれば|いれば|来れば|くれば|読めば|書けば|食べれば|見れば|飲めば|話せば|行けば|作れば|使えば
explanation: One of Japanese's several conditional forms ("if ~, then ~"), made by inflecting a verb's final -u sound to -eba (or an adjective's -i to -kereba). Tends to emphasize a general or hypothetical relationship between the two clauses rather than one specific real event.

examples.japanese: 時間があれば、映画を見に行きたい。
examples.english: If I have time, I'd like to go see a movie.

examples.japanese: この本を読めば、わかりますよ。
examples.english: If you read this book, you'll understand.

matcher: ので|なので
explanation: Attaches after a plain-form clause (or な after a na-adjective/noun) to state a reason leading into a following clause: "since ~, ..." / "because ~, ...". Reads a little softer/more objective than ～から.

examples.japanese: 今日は忙しいので、行けません。
examples.english: Since I'm busy today, I can't go.

examples.japanese: 静かなので、この図書館が好きです。
examples.english: Since it's quiet, I like this library.

matcher: は
explanation: Marks the word before it as the sentence's topic -- what the rest of the sentence is about -- without necessarily saying it's the grammatical subject. Often left untranslated in English.

examples.japanese: わたしは学生です。
examples.english: I am a student.

examples.japanese: この店は魚がおいしい。
examples.english: As for this restaurant, the fish is delicious.

matcher: が
explanation: Marks the word before it as the grammatical subject of the verb or adjective that follows, often introducing new information or answering a "who/what" question, in contrast to は's topic-marking role.

examples.japanese: 猫が窓の外にいます。
examples.english: There is a cat outside the window.

examples.japanese: 誰が来ましたか。
examples.english: Who came?

matcher: を
explanation: Marks the word before it as the direct object of the verb that follows -- the thing being acted on.

examples.japanese: 毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。
examples.english: I drink coffee every morning.

examples.japanese: 公園を散歩しました。
examples.english: I took a walk through the park.

matcher: に
explanation: One small particle covering several related roles: a specific point in time ("at/on"), the location something exists at, the destination of movement ("to"), or the receiver of an action ("to/for someone").

examples.japanese: 七時に起きます。
examples.english: I get up at seven o'clock.

examples.japanese: 友達に手紙を送りました。
examples.english: I sent a letter to my friend.

matcher: で
explanation: Marks either the place where an action happens ("at/in") or the means/tool/method used to do it ("by/with"), distinct from に's marking of a static location of existence.

examples.japanese: 図書館で勉強します。
examples.english: I study at the library.

examples.japanese: バスで学校に行きます。
examples.english: I go to school by bus.

matcher: と
explanation: Links two nouns together as a complete, exhaustive list ("A and B"), or marks the person an action is done together with ("with").

examples.japanese: りんごとみかんを買いました。
examples.english: I bought apples and oranges.

examples.japanese: 友達と映画を見ました。
examples.english: I watched a movie with my friend.

matcher: も
explanation: Replaces は or が to mean "also/too" -- the same thing said about the previous item applies to this one as well.

examples.japanese: わたしは学生です。姉も学生です。
examples.english: I am a student. My older sister is a student too.

examples.japanese: この店はパンもケーキもおいしい。
examples.english: At this shop, both the bread and the cake are delicious.

matcher: から
explanation: Marks a starting point in time or space ("from"), often paired with まで marking the ending point.

examples.japanese: 授業は九時から始まります。
examples.english: Class starts from nine o'clock.

examples.japanese: 東京から大阪まで新幹線で行きました。
examples.english: I went from Tokyo to Osaka by bullet train.

matcher: まで
explanation: Marks an ending point in time or space ("until/up to/as far as"), commonly paired with から marking the starting point.

examples.japanese: 図書館は夜九時まで開いています。
examples.english: The library is open until nine at night.

examples.japanese: ここから駅まで歩いて十分です。
examples.english: It's a ten-minute walk from here to the station.

matcher: や
explanation: Links nouns into a partial, representative list ("A, B, and others") rather than と's complete, exhaustive list -- implies there may be more unmentioned items.

examples.japanese: 机の上にペンやノートがあります。
examples.english: There are things like pens and notebooks on the desk.

examples.japanese: 週末は掃除や洗濯をします。
examples.english: On weekends I do things like cleaning and laundry.

matcher: ですか|ましたか|ますか|でしたか
explanation: Added to the end of a sentence to turn it into a question; Japanese doesn't need to change word order or add a question mark the way English does, so か alone does the whole job.

examples.japanese: これはあなたの傘ですか。
examples.english: Is this your umbrella?

examples.japanese: もう昼ご飯を食べましたか。
examples.english: Have you eaten lunch yet?

matcher: の
explanation: Between two nouns, marks the first as possessing, describing, or specifying the second ("A's B"); after a clause, turns it into a noun-like phrase.

examples.japanese: これはわたしの本です。
examples.english: This is my book.

examples.japanese: 日本語の勉強は楽しいです。
examples.english: Studying Japanese is fun.

matcher: ね
explanation: Added to the end of a sentence to invite agreement or check that the listener shares the same impression, similar to English "..., right?" or "isn't it?".

examples.japanese: 今日はいい天気ですね。
examples.english: It's nice weather today, isn't it?

examples.japanese: このケーキ、おいしいですね。
examples.english: This cake is delicious, right?

matcher: よ
explanation: Added to the end of a sentence to assert something the speaker believes the listener doesn't already know, adding emphasis or a note of "I'm telling you" -- unlike ね, it doesn't invite agreement.

examples.japanese: もう時間ですよ。
examples.english: It's already time, you know.

examples.japanese: その店は今日休みですよ。
examples.english: That shop is closed today, just so you know.

matcher: から
explanation: Attaches after a plain- or polite-form clause to state a direct reason for the clause that follows: "because ~, ...". More subjective/direct-sounding than ので.

examples.japanese: 今日は雨だから、家にいます。
examples.english: Because it's raining today, I'm staying home.

examples.japanese: 眠いから、もう寝ます。
examples.english: Because I'm sleepy, I'm going to sleep now.

matcher: です|だ。
explanation: The copula linking a noun (or na-adjective) to the subject: "is ~". です is the polite form; だ is its plain/casual counterpart, usually dropped entirely in casual speech but kept in writing.

examples.japanese: これは辞書です。
examples.english: This is a dictionary.

examples.japanese: これは辞書だ。
examples.english: This is a dictionary.

matcher: じゃありません|ではありません|じゃない|ではない
explanation: Negates a noun or na-adjective predicate ("is not ~"). ではない is the plainer/more formal-sounding form in writing; じゃない is the common contraction used in speech.

examples.japanese: これは辞書じゃありません。
examples.english: This is not a dictionary.

examples.japanese: 彼は先生ではない。
examples.english: He is not a teacher.

matcher: でした|だった
explanation: Past-tense form of the copula, used after a noun or na-adjective to say something was the case in the past.

examples.japanese: 昨日は休みでした。
examples.english: Yesterday was a day off.

examples.japanese: 学生の頃、彼はサッカー選手だった。
examples.english: Back when he was a student, he was a soccer player.

pattern: ～じゃなかった/～ではなかった
matcher: じゃありませんでした|ではありませんでした|じゃなかった|ではなかった
explanation: Past-negative form of the copula: "was not ~".

examples.japanese: 昨日は休みじゃありませんでした。
examples.english: Yesterday was not a day off.

examples.japanese: それは本当ではなかった。
examples.english: That was not true.

matcher: ます
explanation: The standard polite ending attached to a verb's stem for present/future affirmative statements -- the form learners usually meet first, appropriate in most everyday polite contexts.

examples.japanese: 毎日日本語を勉強します。
examples.english: I study Japanese every day.

examples.japanese: 明日、友達に会います。
examples.english: I will meet my friend tomorrow.

matcher: ません
explanation: The polite negative counterpart of ～ます: "do/does not ~", also used for future negative ("will not ~").

examples.japanese: 朝ご飯を食べません。
examples.english: I don't eat breakfast.

examples.japanese: 今日は学校に行きません。
examples.english: I'm not going to school today.

matcher: ました
explanation: The polite past-tense ending attached to a verb's stem: "did ~ / have done ~".

examples.japanese: 昨日、映画を見ました。
examples.english: I watched a movie yesterday.

examples.japanese: 先週、京都に行きました。
examples.english: I went to Kyoto last week.

matcher: ませんでした
explanation: The polite past-negative ending: "did not ~".

examples.japanese: 昨日は雨が降りませんでした。
examples.english: It did not rain yesterday.

examples.japanese: 朝ご飯を食べませんでした。
examples.english: I did not eat breakfast.

matcher: 食べる|飲む|行く|来る|する|見る|読む|書く|話す
explanation: The base, unconjugated form of a verb, listed as the headword in dictionaries. Used as-is for present/future affirmative in plain/casual speech, and as the base other grammar patterns attach to.

examples.japanese: 明日、映画を見る。
examples.english: I'll watch a movie tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 毎朝コーヒーを飲む。
examples.english: I drink coffee every morning.

matcher: 食べない|飲まない|行かない|来ない|しない|見ない|読まない|書かない|話さない|わからない|知らない
explanation: The plain, casual-speech negative form of a verb (present/future): "don't/doesn't ~". Also the form other patterns like ～ないでください attach to.

examples.japanese: 今日は学校に行かない。
examples.english: I'm not going to school today.

examples.japanese: 辛い食べ物は食べない。
examples.english: I don't eat spicy food.

matcher: 食べた|飲んだ|行った|来た|した|見た|読んだ|書いた|話した
explanation: The plain, casual-speech past-tense form of a verb: "did ~". Also the base other patterns (e.g. ～たり～たりする) attach to.

examples.japanese: 昨日、公園に行った。
examples.english: I went to the park yesterday.

examples.japanese: 朝ご飯を食べた。
examples.english: I ate breakfast.

matcher: 食べなかった|飲まなかった|行かなかった|来なかった|しなかった|見なかった|読まなかった|書かなかった|話さなかった|わからなかった|知らなかった|降らなかった
explanation: The plain, casual-speech past-negative form of a verb: "didn't ~".

examples.japanese: 昨日は雨が降らなかった。
examples.english: It didn't rain yesterday.

examples.japanese: 宿題をしなかった。
examples.english: I didn't do my homework.

matcher: 食べて|飲んで|行って|来て|して|見て|読んで|書いて|話して
explanation: A verb's て-form links it to a following clause or verb, usually describing a sequence of actions ("does A, and then B") -- the same form that also feeds into ～ている, ～てください, and ～てもいい.

examples.japanese: 朝ご飯を食べて、学校に行きます。
examples.english: I eat breakfast, and then go to school.

examples.japanese: 友達と話して、うちに帰りました。
examples.english: I talked with my friend, and then went home.

matcher: てください|でください
explanation: A verb's て-form (で-form for certain verbs) plus ください ("please give me"), used to politely ask or instruct someone to do something: "please ~".

examples.japanese: ここに名前を書いてください。
examples.english: Please write your name here.

examples.japanese: 少し待ってください。
examples.english: Please wait a moment.

matcher: ないでください
explanation: A verb's ない-form plus でください, the negative counterpart of ～てください: "please don't ~".

examples.japanese: ここに車を停めないでください。
examples.english: Please don't park your car here.

examples.japanese: 写真を撮らないでください。
examples.english: Please don't take photos.

matcher: (たり|だり).*(たり|だり)(します|する|しました|した)
explanation: Lists a few representative actions out of a larger, unspecified set, attaching たり after each verb's た-form before a final する: "do things like A and B (among others)".

examples.japanese: 週末は本を読んだり、映画を見たりします。
examples.english: On weekends, I do things like reading books and watching movies.

examples.japanese: 昨日は掃除をしたり、洗濯をしたりした。
examples.english: Yesterday I did things like cleaning and doing laundry.

matcher: ながら
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to say two actions happen at the same time, with the ながら-clause treated as the secondary/background action: "while ~ing".

examples.japanese: 音楽を聞きながら、勉強します。
examples.english: I study while listening to music.

examples.japanese: テレビを見ながら、ご飯を食べました。
examples.english: I ate dinner while watching TV.

matcher: ましょう
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to propose doing something together with the listener: "let's ~".

examples.japanese: 一緒に昼ご飯を食べましょう。
examples.english: Let's eat lunch together.

examples.japanese: 少し休みましょう。
examples.english: Let's take a short break.

matcher: ませんか
explanation: The negative-question form of ～ます used to invite someone to do something, softer and more polite than ～ましょう: "won't you ~?" / "would you like to ~?".

examples.japanese: 今度、一緒に映画を見ませんか。
examples.english: Would you like to watch a movie together sometime?

examples.japanese: お茶でも飲みませんか。
examples.english: Would you like to get some tea (or something)?

matcher: ましょうか
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to offer to do something for the listener or to suggest doing something together, checking their reaction first: "shall I ~?" / "shall we ~?".

examples.japanese: 荷物を持ちましょうか。
examples.english: Shall I carry your bag?

examples.japanese: 窓を開けましょうか。
examples.english: Shall I open the window?

matcher: いです|い。
explanation: An i-adjective describes a noun by itself, without needing a copula, and its dictionary form (ending in い) already carries present-tense affirmative meaning: "is ~".

examples.japanese: このラーメンはおいしいです。
examples.english: This ramen is delicious.

examples.japanese: 今日は寒い。
examples.english: Today is cold.

matcher: くないです|くありません|くない
explanation: Negates an i-adjective by dropping the final い and adding くない (plain) or くないです/くありません (polite): "is not ~".

examples.japanese: このラーメンはおいしくないです。
examples.english: This ramen is not delicious.

examples.japanese: 今日は寒くない。
examples.english: Today is not cold.

matcher: かったです|かった
explanation: Puts an i-adjective into the past tense by dropping the final い and adding かった: "was ~".

examples.japanese: 昨日のテストは難しかったです。
examples.english: Yesterday's test was difficult.

examples.japanese: 去年の夏は暑かった。
examples.english: Last summer was hot.

matcher: くなかったです|くありませんでした|くなかった
explanation: The past-negative form of an i-adjective, made by adding なかった to the く-stem: "was not ~".

examples.japanese: 昨日のテストは難しくなかったです。
examples.english: Yesterday's test was not difficult.

examples.japanese: 去年の夏はあまり暑くなかった。
examples.english: Last summer wasn't very hot.

matcher: 上手です|静かな|きれいな|便利な|好きな|下手な
explanation: A na-adjective needs an extra な when it directly modifies a following noun (unlike i-adjectives, which attach directly), but otherwise conjugates like a noun using です/だ, じゃない, でした, etc.

examples.japanese: 彼女はピアノが上手です。
examples.english: She's good at piano.

examples.japanese: 静かな部屋がほしいです。
examples.english: I want a quiet room.

pattern: ～くなる/～になる (adjective change of state)
matcher: くなりました|くなった|くなる|になりました|になった|になる
explanation: Attaches to an adjective's stem (an i-adjective's く-form, or a na-adjective plus に) plus なる ("become") to describe a change of state: "becomes/got ~".

examples.japanese: 最近、暑くなりました。
examples.english: It's gotten hot recently.

examples.japanese: 練習して、料理が上手になった。
examples.english: I practiced and became good at cooking.

matcher: これ|それ|あれ|どれ
explanation: Pronouns standing in for a thing itself rather than modifying a noun: これ ("this, near the speaker"), それ ("that, near the listener"), あれ ("that, away from both"), どれ ("which one", question word).

examples.japanese: これは私のかばんです。
examples.english: This is my bag.

examples.japanese: どれがあなたの傘ですか。
examples.english: Which one is your umbrella?

matcher: ここ|そこ|あそこ|どこ
explanation: Pronouns for places, following the same near-speaker/near-listener/far-from-both/question pattern as これ/それ/あれ/どれ: "here", "there (near you)", "over there", "where".

examples.japanese: 駅はどこですか。
examples.english: Where is the station?

examples.japanese: ここに座ってください。
examples.english: Please sit here.

pattern: この/その/あの/どの + noun
matcher: この|その|あの|どの
explanation: Unlike これ/それ/あれ/どれ, these always attach directly in front of a noun rather than standing alone: この本 ("this book"), その人 ("that person"), あの店 ("that shop over there"), どの服 ("which clothes").

examples.japanese: この本はとても面白いです。
examples.english: This book is very interesting.

examples.japanese: どの色が好きですか。
examples.english: Which color do you like?

matcher: 何
explanation: The basic question word for things: "what". Read なん before です/だ, counters, and certain consonants, and なに elsewhere (e.g. before を or か).

examples.japanese: これは何ですか。
examples.english: What is this?

examples.japanese: 昼ご飯に何を食べますか。
examples.english: What will you eat for lunch?

matcher: 誰|どなた
explanation: Question words for people: 誰 is the plain form, どなた its more polite equivalent, both meaning "who".

examples.japanese: あの人は誰ですか。
examples.english: Who is that person?

examples.japanese: どなたですか。
examples.english: Who is it (may I ask)?

matcher: いつ
explanation: The question word for time: "when".

examples.japanese: 誕生日はいつですか。
examples.english: When is your birthday?

examples.japanese: いつ日本に行きますか。
examples.english: When are you going to Japan?

matcher: どうして|なぜ
explanation: Question words asking for a reason: "why". どうして is the more common, conversational choice; なぜ sounds a little more formal/written.

examples.japanese: どうして学校を休みましたか。
examples.english: Why did you miss school?

examples.japanese: なぜ日本語を勉強していますか。
examples.english: Why are you studying Japanese?

matcher: どう|どうやって
explanation: Question words asking about manner or method: どう alone often asks for an opinion/impression ("how is it?"), while どうやって specifically asks how to do something ("how/by what method").

examples.japanese: 日本の生活はどうですか。
examples.english: How is life in Japan?

examples.japanese: 駅までどうやって行きますか。
examples.english: How do you get to the station?

matcher: があります|がありました|がない|がありません
explanation: States that an inanimate thing exists somewhere, or that someone has something: "there is ~" / "[someone] has ~". Used for non-living things (plants included) as opposed to います for living things.

examples.japanese: 机の上に本があります。
examples.english: There is a book on the desk.

examples.japanese: 今日は時間がありません。
examples.english: I don't have time today.

matcher: がいます|がいました|がいない|がいません
explanation: States that a living, moving being (a person or animal) exists somewhere: "there is/are ~", the animate counterpart of ～があります.

examples.japanese: 公園に子供がいます。
examples.english: There are children in the park.

examples.japanese: 部屋に猫がいません。
examples.english: There is no cat in the room.

matcher: いくつ|いくら
explanation: いくつ asks "how many" (a general, small-number counter, or someone's age informally), while いくら asks "how much" (price/amount); both fill the slot a counter word would.

examples.japanese: りんごはいくつありますか。
examples.english: How many apples are there?

examples.japanese: このかばんはいくらですか。
examples.english: How much is this bag?

matcher: と思います|と思いました|と思う|と思った
explanation: Attaches after a plain-form clause (the speaker's own quoted thought) plus 思う ("to think"), stating an opinion or guess: "I think that ~".

examples.japanese: 明日は晴れると思います。
examples.english: I think it will be sunny tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 彼はもう帰ったと思う。
examples.english: I think he already went home.

matcher: という|といいます
explanation: Attaches after a name or word to introduce or explain what something is called: "called ~" / "that is to say ~".

examples.japanese: これは「桜」という花です。
examples.english: This is a flower called "sakura".

examples.japanese: 田中さんという人から電話がありました。
examples.english: There was a phone call from a person named Tanaka.

matcher: でしょう
explanation: Attaches after a noun, adjective, or plain-form verb to express the speaker's guess about something, softer/less certain than a plain statement: "probably ~" / "will likely ~".

examples.japanese: 明日は雨でしょう。
examples.english: It will probably rain tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 彼はもう来ないでしょう。
examples.english: He probably won't come anymore.

matcher: 前に
explanation: Attaches after a dictionary-form verb or noun+の to say something happens before another event: "before ~".

examples.japanese: 寝る前に歯を磨きます。
examples.english: I brush my teeth before going to bed.

examples.japanese: 旅行の前に荷物を準備しました。
examples.english: I prepared my luggage before the trip.

matcher: た後で|た後に|の後で|の後に
explanation: Attaches after a verb's た-form (or noun+の) to say something happens after another event: "after ~".

examples.japanese: 宿題をした後で、テレビを見ます。
examples.english: I watch TV after doing my homework.

examples.japanese: 仕事の後で、友達と食事をしました。
examples.english: After work, I had a meal with my friend.

matcher: のが好き|のが上手|のが下手|のが苦手
explanation: Attaches の after a dictionary-form verb to turn the action into a noun phrase ("the act of ~ing"), so adjectives like 好き ("fond of"), 上手 ("good at"), 下手/苦手 ("bad at") can describe it directly.

examples.japanese: 料理を作るのが好きです。
examples.english: I like cooking.

examples.japanese: 彼は歌うのが上手です。
examples.english: He is good at singing.

matcher: たら|だったら|かったら|でしたら
explanation: Attaches to a verb, adjective, or noun's plain past (た) form, meaning "if/when ~ happens, then ...". Often describes a specific one-time condition or a sequence of events ("once ~"), unlike ～ば's more general/hypothetical feel.

examples.japanese: 雨が降ったら、試合は中止になります。
examples.english: If it rains, the game will be canceled.

examples.japanese: 家に着いたら、電話してください。
examples.english: When you get home, please call me.

matcher: なら|ならば
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form clause (or directly to a noun/na-adjective) to mean "if it's the case that ~", often reacting to something already mentioned rather than stating a new hypothesis. Frequently used to give advice based on the other person's situation.

examples.japanese: 東京に行くなら、新幹線が便利です。
examples.english: If you're going to Tokyo, the shinkansen is convenient.

examples.japanese: 高いなら、買わなくてもいいです。
examples.english: If it's expensive, you don't have to buy it.

matcher: すると|なると|来ると|くると|押すと|食べると|飲むと|見ると|聞くと|使うと|行くと|帰ると|入ると|出ると
explanation: A verb's plain non-past form plus と states that the second clause automatically or naturally follows the first: "whenever ~ happens, ...". Common for natural laws, habitual results, and mechanical cause-and-effect, and can't be used to make a request or suggestion in the second clause.

examples.japanese: このボタンを押すと、電気がつきます。
examples.english: If you press this button, the light turns on.

examples.japanese: 春になると、桜が咲きます。
examples.english: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.

matcher: てあげます|てあげました|てあげる|てあげて
explanation: Attaches to a verb's て-form to show the speaker (or someone in their in-group) does an action as a favor for someone else. Can sound slightly self-important toward the listener directly, so it's used carefully depending on who benefits.

examples.japanese: 友達に日本語を教えてあげました。
examples.english: I taught my friend Japanese, as a favor to them.

examples.japanese: 荷物を持ってあげますよ。
examples.english: I'll carry your luggage for you.

matcher: てくれます|てくれました|てくれる|てくれた
explanation: Attaches to a verb's て-form to show someone else does an action as a favor toward the speaker (or the speaker's in-group), expressing gratitude built into the grammar itself rather than a separate word.

examples.japanese: 友達が駅まで迎えに来てくれました。
examples.english: My friend came to meet me at the station, for my benefit.

examples.japanese: 先生が丁寧に説明してくれる。
examples.english: The teacher explains things carefully for us.

matcher: てもらいます|てもらいました|てもらう|てもらった
explanation: Attaches to a verb's て-form, framed from the receiver's viewpoint: the speaker has someone else do an action as a favor for them, roughly "I get/had [someone] do ~ for me".

examples.japanese: 友達に空港まで送ってもらいました。
examples.english: I had my friend drive me to the airport.

examples.japanese: 先生に作文を直してもらう。
examples.english: I get my essay corrected by the teacher.

matcher: られます|られない|られる|食べられる|見られる|来られる|こられる|読める|書ける|飲める|行ける|使える|泳げる|帰れる|帰れない|話せる
explanation: A verb's potential form, expressing that an action is possible for the subject to do: "can ~". Ichidan verbs and 来る take ～られる, godan verbs change their final -u sound to -eru, and する becomes できる.

examples.japanese: この魚は生でも食べられます。
examples.english: This fish can be eaten raw too.

examples.japanese: 忙しくて、今日は早く帰れない。
examples.english: I'm busy, so I can't go home early today.

matcher: れています|れました|られました|られる|れる
explanation: A verb's passive form, shifting focus onto the person or thing an action happens to: "is done to ~" / "was ~ed". Also commonly used for actions that inconvenience or affect the speaker, even with intransitive verbs, unlike the English passive.

examples.japanese: この本は多くの人に読まれています。
examples.english: This book is read by many people.

examples.japanese: 子供の頃、よく兄にいじめられました。
examples.english: When I was a kid, I was often picked on by my older brother.

matcher: させます|させました|させる|読ませました|読ませる|書かせる|行かせる|待たせる|働かせる|歩かせる
explanation: A verb's causative form, meaning the subject makes or lets someone else do an action: "make/let [someone] ~". Ichidan verbs and する take ～させる, while godan verbs change their final -u sound to -aseru.

examples.japanese: 母は毎日、妹に部屋を掃除させます。
examples.english: My mother makes my little sister clean her room every day.

examples.japanese: 先生は学生に本を読ませました。
examples.english: The teacher had the students read the book.

matcher: させられます|させられました|させられる|たされた|たされました|たされる
explanation: Combines the causative and passive forms to describe being made to do something against one's own will: "was made to ~". For godan verbs this often contracts (e.g. 待たせられる becomes 待たされる).

examples.japanese: 子供の頃、嫌いな野菜を食べさせられました。
examples.english: As a kid, I was made to eat vegetables I hated.

examples.japanese: 上司に長い時間、会議で待たされた。
examples.english: My boss made me wait a long time in the meeting.

matcher: そうです|そうな|そうに|そうだった|そうだ
explanation: Attaches to an adjective's stem (dropping い) or a verb's stem to describe how something looks or seems based on the speaker's own visual impression: "looks like ~" / "seems ~". Distinct from ～らしい, which reports something the speaker heard.

examples.japanese: このケーキ、とても美味しそうですね。
examples.english: This cake looks really delicious.

examples.japanese: 今にも雨が降りそうな空だ。
examples.english: The sky looks like it's about to rain any moment.

matcher: そうです|そうだ|そうでした
explanation: Attaches directly to a plain-form verb, adjective, or noun+だ to report information the speaker learned from someone else or from a source like the news: "I hear that ~". Unlike ～そう (appearance), this attaches to the full plain form rather than a stem.

examples.japanese: 天気予報によると、明日は晴れるそうです。
examples.english: According to the weather forecast, I hear it'll be sunny tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 彼はもう会社を辞めたそうだ。
examples.english: I heard he already quit his company.

matcher: すぎます|すぎました|すぎる|すぎた
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem or an adjective's stem to mean the action or quality goes too far: "too much ~" / "over-~". Behaves like an ordinary ichidan verb once attached, so it can itself take past tense, negative, and other endings.

examples.japanese: 昨日は食べすぎました。
examples.english: Yesterday I ate too much.

examples.japanese: この問題は難しすぎる。
examples.english: This problem is too difficult.

matcher: ようです|ようだ|ような|ように
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form clause (or noun+の) to express the speaker's own conjecture or impression based on evidence, or to compare something to something else: "it seems ~" / "like ~". More neutral and slightly more formal-sounding than the casual ～みたい.

examples.japanese: 彼はまだ事情を知らないようです。
examples.english: It seems he doesn't know the situation yet.

examples.japanese: 外はまるで冬のように寒い。
examples.english: Outside it's cold, just like winter.

matcher: みたいです|みたいな|みたいに|みたいだ
explanation: The casual-speech counterpart of ～ようだ, attaching directly to a plain-form clause or noun to express conjecture or resemblance: "seems like ~" / "like ~". Common in everyday conversation, less common in writing.

examples.japanese: あの人、日本人みたいですね。
examples.english: That person seems like they're Japanese, doesn't he.

examples.japanese: 子供みたいに泣かないでよ。
examples.english: Don't cry like a child.

matcher: かもしれません|かもしれない|かも知れない
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form clause to mark a weak possibility the speaker isn't sure about: "might ~" / "maybe ~". Weaker in certainty than ～はずだ or ～でしょう.

examples.japanese: 明日は雪が降るかもしれません。
examples.english: It might snow tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 彼は今日、来ないかもしれない。
examples.english: He might not come today.

matcher: はずです|はずだ|はずがない|はずはない
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form clause to state a confident expectation based on evidence or logic, rather than a guess: "should be ~" / "is supposed to ~". The negative ～はずがない means "there's no way that ~" -- a strong denial, not just "probably not".

examples.japanese: 田中さんはもう着いているはずです。
examples.english: Mr. Tanaka should have already arrived.

examples.japanese: 彼が嘘をつくはずがない。
examples.english: There's no way he would lie.

matcher: つもりです|つもりだ|つもりはない|つもりで
explanation: Attaches to a verb's dictionary or negative form to state the speaker's (or, in questions/reports, someone else's) firm intention or plan: "intend to ~" / "plan to ~".

examples.japanese: 来年、大学院に進学するつもりです。
examples.english: I intend to go on to graduate school next year.

examples.japanese: 彼女は会社を辞めるつもりはないらしい。
examples.english: Apparently she has no intention of quitting the company.

matcher: ておきます|ておきました|ておく|ておいて|といて|とく
explanation: Attaches to a verb's て-form to mean doing something in advance, for later benefit, or leaving something in a certain state on purpose: "do ~ in advance" / "leave it as ~". Often contracted to ～とく/～といて in casual speech.

examples.japanese: 明日の会議のために、資料を準備しておきます。
examples.english: I'll prepare the materials in advance for tomorrow's meeting.

examples.japanese: ドアを開けといて。
examples.english: Leave the door open, would you.

matcher: てしまいます|てしまいました|てしまう|ちゃう|じゃう|ちゃった|じゃった
explanation: Attaches to a verb's て-form to emphasize an action is completely finished, or to add a nuance of regret about something that happened unintentionally: "end up ~ing" / "go and ~". Commonly contracted to ～ちゃう/～じゃう in casual speech.

examples.japanese: 大事な書類を無くしてしまいました。
examples.english: I ended up losing an important document.

examples.japanese: そのケーキ、もう食べちゃったの?
examples.english: Did you already go and eat that cake?

matcher: てみます|てみました|てみる|てみたい|てみて
explanation: Attaches to a verb's て-form (literally "try doing and see") to mean trying an action out to see what happens: "try ~ing". Different from English "try to ~", since here the action is actually carried out, not just attempted.

examples.japanese: 新しいレストランに行ってみます。
examples.english: I'll try going to the new restaurant.

examples.japanese: このドレスを着てみてもいいですか。
examples.english: May I try on this dress?

matcher: ながら
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to join two actions the same subject does at the same time, with the main clause's action as the primary focus: "while ~ing".

examples.japanese: 音楽を聞きながら、宿題をします。
examples.english: I do my homework while listening to music.

examples.japanese: 彼はいつも笑いながら話す。
examples.english: He always talks while laughing.

matcher: のに
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form clause to join two clauses whose relationship goes against expectation: "even though ~" / "despite ~". Often carries a nuance of surprise, disappointment, or complaint that ～けど doesn't necessarily have.

examples.japanese: 一生懸命勉強したのに、試験に落ちてしまった。
examples.english: Even though I studied hard, I still failed the exam.

examples.japanese: 雨なのに、彼は傘を持っていない。
examples.english: Even though it's raining, he doesn't have an umbrella.

matcher: するな|来るな|くるな|行くな|食べるな|飲むな|見るな|言うな|忘れるな|開けるな|触るな|入るな
explanation: Attaches directly to a verb's plain non-past (dictionary) form to give a blunt, forceful prohibition: "don't ~!". Much stronger and more direct than ～ないでください, typically used by someone with authority, in anger, or in signs/warnings.

examples.japanese: ここに入るな。
examples.english: Don't come in here.

examples.japanese: 危ないから、触るな!
examples.english: It's dangerous, so don't touch it!

matcher: しよう|行こう|食べよう|飲もう|見よう|話そう|読もう|書こう|作ろう|使おう|待とう|帰ろう
explanation: A verb's volitional form, made by changing a godan verb's final -u sound to -ou or an ichidan verb's る to よう, expressing the speaker's own resolve or a casual suggestion: "let's ~" / "I'll ~".

examples.japanese: そろそろ帰ろう。
examples.english: Let's head home soon.

examples.japanese: 今度の週末、映画を見よう。
examples.english: Let's watch a movie this coming weekend.

matcher: ようと思います|ようと思った|ようと思う|ようと思って
explanation: Combines a verb's volitional form with 思う ("to think") to express the speaker's own tentative plan or intention, formed in the moment rather than a firm long-standing decision: "I'm thinking of ~ing".

examples.japanese: 来年、留学しようと思っています。
examples.english: I'm thinking of studying abroad next year.

examples.japanese: 週末は家でゆっくりしようと思う。
examples.english: I'm thinking I'll just relax at home this weekend.

matcher: るところです|るところだ|たところです|たところだ|ているところです|ているところだ
explanation: Attaches after a verb's dictionary form, た-form, or ～ている form to pinpoint exactly where an action stands in time: about to start, just finished, or currently in progress, depending on which form precedes it.

examples.japanese: 今、ちょうど出かけるところです。
examples.english: I'm just about to head out right now.

examples.japanese: 会議はさっき終わったところだ。
examples.english: The meeting just ended a moment ago.

matcher: たばかりです|たばかりだ|たばかりで|たばかりの
explanation: Attaches to a verb's plain past (た) form to emphasize that something happened only recently, from the speaker's subjective sense of "just now": "just ~ed".

examples.japanese: この会社に入ったばかりで、まだ何もわかりません。
examples.english: I just joined this company, so I still don't understand anything.

examples.japanese: 引っ越したばかりの部屋はまだ片付いていない。
examples.english: The room I just moved into isn't tidied up yet.

matcher: てほしいです|てほしい|てほしかった
explanation: Attaches to a verb's て-form to express that the speaker wants someone else to do something: "I want [someone] to ~". A verb-based counterpart to ～たい, which can only describe the speaker's own desire to act.

examples.japanese: もっと野菜を食べてほしいです。
examples.english: I want you to eat more vegetables.

examples.japanese: 彼にはもっと早く来てほしかった。
examples.english: I wanted him to come earlier.

matcher: べきです|べきだ|べきではない|べきじゃない
explanation: Attaches to a verb's dictionary form to state what the speaker believes ought to be done, as a matter of duty or good judgment: "should ~". Carries more moral or normative weight than casual advice.

examples.japanese: 約束は守るべきです。
examples.english: You should keep your promises.

examples.japanese: そんなことをするべきではない。
examples.english: You shouldn't do something like that.

matcher: んです|んだ|のです|なんです
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form clause to frame a statement as an explanation, background reason, or something the speaker wants to clarify, rather than a plain fact: roughly "the thing is, ~". Very common in spoken Japanese, often contracted from ～のです to ～んです.

examples.japanese: 頭が痛いんです。
examples.english: The thing is, I have a headache.

examples.japanese: 実は、来月結婚するんです。
examples.english: Actually, I'm getting married next month.

matcher: 降っても|頑張っても|しても|食べても|飲んでも|行っても|来ても|きても|見ても|話しても|読んでも|書いても|使っても
explanation: Attaches to a verb's て-form plus も to mean "even if ~" / "no matter ~", stating that the following clause holds true regardless of the first clause's condition.

examples.japanese: 雨が降っても、試合は行われます。
examples.english: Even if it rains, the match will be held.

examples.japanese: いくら頑張っても、うまくいかなかった。
examples.english: No matter how hard I tried, it didn't go well.

matcher: 場合は|場合、|場合に|場合でも
explanation: Attaches after a plain-form clause (literally "in the case that ~") to introduce a specific, often less likely, scenario and what should happen in it: "in the event that ~" / "if it turns out that ~". Common in instructions and formal notices.

examples.japanese: 遅れる場合は、必ず連絡してください。
examples.english: If you're going to be late, please be sure to contact me.

examples.japanese: 台風が来た場合、学校は休みになります。
examples.english: In the event a typhoon comes, school will be canceled.

matcher: 間に|ている間|いる間
explanation: Attaches after a clause describing an ongoing state or period to mark a window of time during which something else happens: "while ~" / "during ~". ～間に (with に) marks a one-time event happening within that window, while bare ～間 marks something continuous throughout it.

examples.japanese: 子供が寝ている間に、家事を済ませます。
examples.english: While the kids are asleep, I get the housework done.

examples.japanese: 日本にいる間に、いろいろな場所を旅行したい。
examples.english: While I'm in Japan, I want to travel to various places.

matcher: 前に
explanation: Attaches after a verb's dictionary form (regardless of the sentence's own tense) to mean "before ~ing", marking one action as happening prior to another.

examples.japanese: 寝る前に、歯を磨きます。
examples.english: I brush my teeth before going to sleep.

examples.japanese: 日本に来る前に、少し日本語を勉強しました。
examples.english: Before coming to Japan, I studied a little Japanese.

matcher: 後で|た後に|た後
explanation: Attaches after a verb's plain past (た) form to mean "after ~ing", marking one action as happening once another has finished.

examples.japanese: 宿題を終えた後で、テレビを見ます。
examples.english: After finishing my homework, I watch TV.

examples.japanese: 卒業した後、すぐに就職した。
examples.english: Right after graduating, I got a job immediately.

matcher: ために|ための|ためです
explanation: Attaches after a dictionary-form verb (or noun+の) to state a purpose or goal being worked toward: "in order to ~" / "for the sake of ~". With a noun-only cause instead of a purpose, it can also mean "because of ~".

examples.japanese: 健康のために、毎朝走っています。
examples.english: For the sake of my health, I run every morning.

examples.japanese: 試験に合格するために、毎日勉強している。
examples.english: In order to pass the exam, I study every day.

matcher: 予定です|予定だ|予定で|予定はない
explanation: Attaches after a verb's dictionary form (or noun+の) to describe a scheduled or already-arranged plan, more concrete than ～つもり's personal intention: "is scheduled to ~" / "planned to ~".

examples.japanese: 来月、大阪へ出張する予定です。
examples.english: I'm scheduled to go on a business trip to Osaka next month.

examples.japanese: 今年は海外旅行に行く予定はない。
examples.english: I have no plans to travel abroad this year.

matcher: ことにします|ことにしました|ことにする|ことにした
explanation: Attaches after a verb's dictionary or negative form to mark a decision the speaker has actively made: "I've decided to ~". Contrasts with ～ことになる, where the outcome comes about rather than being chosen.

examples.japanese: 来月からジムに通うことにしました。
examples.english: I've decided to start going to the gym from next month.

examples.japanese: 今日は早く寝ることにする。
examples.english: I've decided to go to sleep early today.

matcher: ことになります|ことになりました|ことになる|ことになっている
explanation: Attaches after a verb's dictionary or negative form to describe a decision or arrangement that came about, often made by someone else or by circumstances rather than the speaker: "it's been decided that ~" / "it turns out that ~".

examples.japanese: 来年、大阪に転勤することになりました。
examples.english: It's been decided that I'll be transferred to Osaka next year.

examples.japanese: 会議は来週の月曜日に行われることになっている。
examples.english: It's been arranged that the meeting will be held next Monday.

matcher: ようにします|ようにしました|ようにしています|ようにする|ようにしている|ようにしましょう
explanation: Attaches after a verb's dictionary or negative form to describe making an ongoing effort to reach or maintain a certain habit or state: "try to make sure to ~" / "make it a habit to ~".

examples.japanese: 毎日野菜を食べるようにしています。
examples.english: I make an effort to eat vegetables every day.

examples.japanese: 遅刻しないようにしましょう。
examples.english: Let's make sure not to be late.

matcher: ように言いました|ように言う|ように言って|ように言われた|ように言われました
explanation: Attaches after a verb's dictionary or negative form before 言う ("say") or a similar reporting verb to relay an instruction or request given to someone else: "told [someone] to ~".

examples.japanese: 先生は学生に静かにするように言いました。
examples.english: The teacher told the students to be quiet.

examples.japanese: 母に早く帰るように言われた。
examples.english: I was told by my mother to come home early.

matcher: させてください|させて下さい|[かがさざただなばまらわ]せてください
explanation: Combines the causative form with ～てください to have the speaker politely ask for permission to do something themselves: "please let me ~". Softer and more humble-sounding than simply announcing what one is going to do.

examples.japanese: すみません、少し休ませてください。
examples.english: Excuse me, please let me rest a little.

examples.japanese: 一度、自分でやらせてください。
examples.english: Please let me try doing it myself once.

matcher: しかない|しかありません|しかいない|しかできない
explanation: Attaches after a noun or verb, always paired with a negative predicate, to mean "only ~" -- often with a nuance that the amount or option is felt to be insufficient, unlike the more neutral ～だけ.

examples.japanese: 財布には千円しかありません。
examples.english: I only have a thousand yen in my wallet.

examples.japanese: この部屋には椅子が一つしかない。
examples.english: There's only one chair in this room.

matcher: (たり|だり).+(たり|だり)し(ます|ました|た|て|ている|ていた)
explanation: Lists two or more representative actions or states out of a larger, unordered set of things someone does, using each verb's plain past (た/だ) form plus り: "do things like ~ and ~". Implies there are other, unlisted actions too, unlike ～て listing every action in sequence.

examples.japanese: 週末は本を読んだり、映画を見たりします。
examples.english: On weekends, I do things like read books and watch movies.

examples.japanese: 子供たちは公園で走ったり、笑ったりしていた。
examples.english: The kids were running around, laughing, and so on at the park.

matcher: 方が分かりません|方を教えて|作り方|使い方|読み方|書き方|やり方|行き方
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to turn it into a noun meaning "the way of ~ing" / "how to ~", commonly followed by わかる or 教える.

examples.japanese: この漢字の読み方がわかりません。
examples.english: I don't know how to read this kanji.

examples.japanese: 新しい機械の使い方を教えてください。
examples.english: Please teach me how to use the new machine.

matcher: やすいです|やすい|やすかった
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to mean the action is easy to do: "easy to ~". Behaves like an ordinary い-adjective once attached.

examples.japanese: このペンはとても書きやすいです。
examples.english: This pen is very easy to write with.

examples.japanese: 分かりやすい説明、ありがとうございます。
examples.english: Thank you for the easy-to-understand explanation.

matcher: にくいです|にくい|にくかった
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to mean the action is difficult or awkward to do: "hard to ~". The direct opposite of ～やすい, and likewise behaves like an い-adjective once attached.

examples.japanese: この靴は少し歩きにくいです。
examples.english: These shoes are a bit hard to walk in.

examples.japanese: 彼の字は読みにくい。
examples.english: His handwriting is hard to read.

matcher: 続けます|続けました|続けています|続ける|続けている|続けた
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to mean continuing to do that action over a stretch of time: "keep ~ing" / "continue to ~".

examples.japanese: 彼はもう十年、日本語を勉強し続けています。
examples.english: He's been continuing to study Japanese for ten years now.

examples.japanese: 疲れても、最後まで走り続けた。
examples.english: Even though I was tired, I kept running until the end.

matcher: 出します|出しました|出す|出した
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to mean an action starts suddenly or unexpectedly: "suddenly start ~ing". Carries more of a sense of abruptness than the more neutral ～始める.

examples.japanese: 赤ちゃんが急に泣き出しました。
examples.english: The baby suddenly started crying.

examples.japanese: 空が暗くなって、雨が降り出した。
examples.english: The sky grew dark, and it started raining.

matcher: 始めます|始めました|始める|始めた
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to mark the beginning of an action or ongoing process, without the suddenness implied by ～出す: "start ~ing" / "begin to ~".

examples.japanese: 三年前からギターを習い始めました。
examples.english: I started learning guitar three years ago.

examples.japanese: 彼女は去年、小説を書き始めた。
examples.english: She started writing a novel last year.

matcher: 終わります|終わりました|終わる|終わった
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to mark the completion of an action: "finish ~ing".

examples.japanese: この本はもう読み終わりました。
examples.english: I've already finished reading this book.

examples.japanese: レポートを書き終わったら、寝ます。
examples.english: Once I finish writing the report, I'll go to sleep.

matcher: けれども|けれど|だけど|けど
explanation: Attaches after a plain- or polite-form clause to join two contrasting ideas: "but ~" / "although ~". ～けど is the casual-speech contraction of ～けれど/～けれども.

examples.japanese: この店は安いけれど、あまり美味しくない。
examples.english: This restaurant is cheap, but it's not very tasty.

examples.japanese: 行きたいけど、時間がない。
examples.english: I want to go, but I don't have time.

matcher: いし、|るし、|だし、|たし、
explanation: Attaches after a plain-form clause to list one reason or fact among possibly several others, all pointing toward the same conclusion: "~, and also ~". Usually implies there's more that could be added.

examples.japanese: この店は安いし、美味しいし、いつも混んでいる。
examples.english: This place is cheap, it's tasty, and it's always crowded.

examples.japanese: 今日は雨だし、家でゆっくりしよう。
examples.english: It's raining today, so let's just relax at home.

matcher: でしょう|だろう
explanation: Attaches after a plain-form clause to state a probable outcome the speaker is fairly, but not completely, confident about: "probably ~" / "will likely ~". ～だろう is the plain-speech equivalent of polite ～でしょう.

examples.japanese: 明日は晴れるでしょう。
examples.english: It will probably be sunny tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 彼はもう知っているだろう。
examples.english: He probably already knows.

matcher: お.+になります|お.+になりました|お.+になる|ご.+になります|ご.+になる
explanation: Wraps a verb's stem (お + stem + になる, or ご + a Sino-Japanese noun-verb + になる) to raise up the person doing the action, out of respect: honorific speech used for a listener or third party of higher status, never for the speaker's own actions.

examples.japanese: 社長はもうお帰りになりました。
examples.english: The president has already gone home.

examples.japanese: こちらの資料をご覧になりますか。
examples.english: Would you like to look over these materials?

matcher: お.+します|お.+いたします|お.+した|ご.+します|ご.+いたします
explanation: Wraps a verb's stem (お + stem + する, or ご + a Sino-Japanese noun-verb + する) to lower the speaker's own action out of humility toward the listener: humble speech used only for the speaker's own actions, the mirror image of お～になる.

examples.japanese: 荷物をお持ちします。
examples.english: I will carry your luggage.

examples.japanese: 詳しくご説明いたします。
examples.english: I will explain in detail.

matcher: とき|時、|時に
explanation: Attaches after a plain-form clause, adjective, or noun+の to mark the time at which something happens or happened: "when ~". The tense of the clause before とき matters: a past-tense verb before とき means the main action happened after that event, not before it.

examples.japanese: 暇なときに、映画を見に行きます。
examples.english: When I have free time, I go watch movies.

examples.japanese: 子供の時、よくこの公園で遊びました。
examples.english: When I was a kid, I often played in this park.

matcher: なくてもいいです|なくてもいい|なくてもかまわない
explanation: Attaches to a verb's negative stem plus て-form (drop the final い of ～ない, add くて) to mean an action isn't required: "don't have to ~" / "it's fine not to ~". The negative counterpart of ～なければならない.

examples.japanese: 今日は残業しなくてもいいです。
examples.english: You don't have to work overtime today.

examples.japanese: 心配しなくてもいいよ。
examples.english: You don't need to worry.

matcher: ないでください|ないで
explanation: Attaches to a verb's negative stem to mean either "without ~ing" (joining a second clause) or, with ください, a direct negative request: "please don't ~".

examples.japanese: 写真を撮らないでください。
examples.english: Please don't take photos.

examples.japanese: 朝ご飯を食べないで、学校に行った。
examples.english: I went to school without eating breakfast.

matcher: たことがあります|たことがある|たことがあった|たことがない|ことがあります|ことがある
explanation: After a verb's plain past (た) form, states that the speaker has had the experience of doing something at least once: "have ~ed before". After a verb's plain non-past form instead, it means something happens on occasion rather than describing an experience: "sometimes ~s".

examples.japanese: 一度だけ富士山に登ったことがあります。
examples.english: I've climbed Mt. Fuji just once.

examples.japanese: 彼は時々、朝ごはんを抜くことがある。
examples.english: He sometimes skips breakfast.

matcher: 子供でも|初心者でも|誰でも|何でも|いつでも
explanation: Attaches directly after a noun to mean "even ~", emphasizing an extreme example to make a broader point ("even a beginner can do this, so anyone can"). Also combines with question words (誰でも, 何でも, いつでも) to mean "anyone/anything/anytime at all".

examples.japanese: このアプリは子供でも簡単に使えます。
examples.english: Even a child can use this app easily.

examples.japanese: 誰でも参加できるイベントです。
examples.english: This is an event that anyone can participate in.

matcher: とおりに|通りに|とおりの|通りの
explanation: Attaches after a verb's dictionary or plain past form (or noun+の) to mean doing something exactly as specified or shown: "just as ~" / "according to ~".

examples.japanese: 先生が言ったとおりにやってみました。
examples.english: I tried doing it just as the teacher said.

examples.japanese: レシピの通りに作れば、失敗しません。
examples.english: If you make it according to the recipe, you won't fail.

matcher: (て|で)ばかりいます|(て|で)ばかりいました|(て|で)ばかりいる|(て|で)ばかりいない|(て|で)ばかりだ
explanation: Attaches to a verb's て-form to criticize someone for doing one thing excessively, to the exclusion of everything else they should be doing: "do nothing but ~" / "always just ~ing".

examples.japanese: 彼は最近、遊んでばかりいる。
examples.english: Lately he does nothing but play around.

examples.japanese: テレビを見てばかりいないで、勉強しなさい。
examples.english: Don't just sit there watching TV all the time -- study.

matcher: わけです|わけだ
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form clause to state a logical conclusion that naturally follows from what's already been said: "so it means that ~" / "no wonder ~". Frames the statement as an inference from known facts, not new information.

examples.japanese: 毎日3時間も練習しているんだから、上手になるわけだ。
examples.english: Since he practices three hours every day, no wonder he's getting good.

examples.japanese: 彼女はロンドンで10年間暮らしていた。だから英語が上手なわけです。
examples.english: She lived in London for ten years. That's why her English is good.

matcher: わけではない|わけじゃない|わけではありません
explanation: Negates わけだ's "it naturally follows that" to mean "it's not that ~" / "that doesn't necessarily mean ~" -- softening a conclusion someone might otherwise wrongly draw.

examples.japanese: 甘いものが嫌いなわけではないが、最近は控えている。
examples.english: It's not that I dislike sweets, but I've been cutting back on them lately.

examples.japanese: 全員が反対したわけではありません。数人は賛成していました。
examples.english: It's not that everyone was against it -- a few people were in favor.

matcher: はずがない|はずはない|はずがありません
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form clause to strongly deny a possibility based on the speaker's reasoning: "there's no way ~" / "it can't be that ~".

examples.japanese: あの真面目な田中さんが遅刻するはずがない。
examples.english: There's no way serious Mr. Tanaka would be late.

examples.japanese: こんな値段でこんなに質のいい物が買えるはずがありません。
examples.english: There's no way you can buy something this good quality at this price.

matcher: に違いない|に違いありません
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form clause to express the speaker's confident conviction, based on evidence, that something must be true: "it must be ~" / "no doubt ~".

examples.japanese: この足跡の大きさからすると、犯人は男性に違いない。
examples.english: Judging by the size of these footprints, the culprit must be a man.

examples.japanese: 部屋の電気がついている。誰か家にいるに違いない。
examples.english: The light in the room is on. Someone must be home.

matcher: てばかりいる|てばかりいます|てばかりいた|てばかりいて
explanation: Attaches to a verb's て-form to criticize a habit of doing only that one thing, to the exclusion of everything else: "does nothing but ~" / "is always ~ing".

examples.japanese: 息子はゲームをしてばかりいて、全然勉強しない。
examples.english: My son does nothing but play video games and never studies at all.

examples.japanese: そんなに文句を言ってばかりいると、誰も手伝ってくれなくなるよ。
examples.english: If you keep doing nothing but complain, no one will help you anymore.

matcher: ばかりに
explanation: Attaches to a clause to blame an unfortunate result entirely on that one cause: "just because ~" / "all because of ~", usually with regret.

examples.japanese: 財布を忘れたばかりに、昼ご飯を食べられなかった。
examples.english: Just because I forgot my wallet, I couldn't eat lunch.

examples.japanese: 近道をしようとしたばかりに、かえって時間がかかってしまった。
examples.english: All because I tried to take a shortcut, it ended up taking even longer.

matcher: 上に
explanation: Attaches to a clause to add a second, similarly-weighted fact on top of the first, both usually positive or both negative: "on top of ~ing" / "not only ~ but also".

examples.japanese: このレストランは料理がおいしい上に、値段も安い。
examples.english: Not only is the food at this restaurant delicious, it's also cheap.

examples.japanese: 道が混んでいた上に、雨まで降り出した。
examples.english: On top of the roads being congested, it even started raining.

matcher: るところです|るところだ|るところでした
explanation: Attaches to a verb's dictionary form plus ところ ("point/moment") plus だ, marking that the action is just about to happen: "is just about to ~".

examples.japanese: 今から出かけるところです。
examples.english: I'm just about to head out now.

examples.japanese: 電話が鳴った時、ちょうど寝るところだった。
examples.english: When the phone rang, I was just about to go to sleep.

matcher: ているところです|ているところだ|ているところでした
explanation: Attaches to a verb's て-form plus いる plus ところだ, marking that the action is currently in progress right now: "is in the middle of ~ing".

examples.japanese: 今、資料を準備しているところです。
examples.english: Right now, I'm in the middle of preparing the materials.

examples.japanese: 彼が来た時、私はちょうど夕食を作っているところだった。
examples.english: When he arrived, I was just in the middle of making dinner.

matcher: たところです|たところだ|たところでした
explanation: Attaches to a verb's plain past (た) form plus ところだ, marking that the action has just finished: "just did ~" / "have just ~ed".

examples.japanese: ちょうど今、レポートを書き終えたところです。
examples.english: I just finished writing the report right now.

examples.japanese: 彼は先月、この町に引っ越してきたところだ。
examples.english: He just moved to this town last month.

matcher: たとたんに|たとたん
explanation: Attaches to a verb's plain past (た) form to mark that a second event happened immediately, often surprisingly, right at that instant: "the moment ~, ..." / "just as soon as ~".

examples.japanese: ドアを開けたとたんに、猫が飛び出してきた。
examples.english: The moment I opened the door, the cat jumped out.

examples.japanese: 彼の顔を見たとたん、涙が止まらなくなった。
examples.english: The instant I saw his face, I couldn't stop crying.

matcher: に伴って|に伴い|に伴う
explanation: Attaches to a noun or clause describing a change, marking a second change that occurs alongside it: "along with ~" / "as ~ progresses".

examples.japanese: 人口の増加に伴って、住宅の需要も高まっている。
examples.english: Along with the population increase, demand for housing is also rising.

examples.japanese: 技術の進歩に伴い、私たちの生活は大きく変わった。
examples.english: As technology has advanced, our lives have changed greatly.

matcher: に応じて|に応じた|に応じ
explanation: Attaches to a noun marking a varying condition, meaning that something adjusts to match it: "according to ~" / "in response to ~".

examples.japanese: 収入に応じて、税金の額が変わる。
examples.english: The amount of tax changes according to one's income.

examples.japanese: お客様のご要望に応じて、メニューを調整いたします。
examples.english: We'll adjust the menu in response to the customer's requests.

matcher: としたら|とすれば|とすると
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form clause to set up a hypothetical premise and reason from it: "if we suppose ~" / "assuming ~, then...".

examples.japanese: もし宝くじが当たったとしたら、何に使いますか。
examples.english: If we suppose you won the lottery, what would you use it for?

examples.japanese: 明日雨が降るとすれば、試合は中止になるだろう。
examples.english: Assuming it rains tomorrow, the game will probably be canceled.

matcher: にしては
explanation: Attaches to a noun or plain-form clause to note that something doesn't match the usual expectation set by it: "for ~" / "considering ~, surprisingly...".

examples.japanese: 彼は初心者にしては、なかなか上手にスキーを滑る。
examples.english: For a beginner, he skis pretty well.

examples.japanese: 今日は5月にしては、ずいぶん寒いですね。
examples.english: For May, it's quite cold today, isn't it.

matcher: にしても
explanation: Attaches to a noun or plain-form clause to concede a point and note that it doesn't change the conclusion: "even granting ~" / "even if we say ~".

examples.japanese: 忙しいにしても、返信ぐらいはできるはずだ。
examples.english: Even granting that you're busy, you should at least be able to reply.

examples.japanese: 冗談にしても、あの言い方はひどすぎる。
examples.english: Even if it was a joke, that way of saying it was too harsh.

matcher: に対して|に対する|に対し
explanation: Attaches to a noun marking the target of an attitude, action, or contrast: "toward ~" / "in contrast to ~".

examples.japanese: 先生は生徒たちに対して、いつも優しく接している。
examples.english: The teacher always treats the students kindly.

examples.japanese: 兄が社交的なのに対して、弟はとても内向的だ。
examples.english: In contrast to his older brother being sociable, the younger brother is very introverted.

matcher: に関して|に関する|に関し
explanation: Attaches to a noun marking the topic something concerns: "regarding ~" / "concerning ~", a slightly formal alternative to について.

examples.japanese: 今回の事故に関して、詳しい報告書が提出された。
examples.english: Regarding this accident, a detailed report was submitted.

examples.japanese: 環境問題に関する本を何冊か読んでみた。
examples.english: I read a few books concerning environmental issues.

matcher: というのは
explanation: Marks a word or clause as the topic being explained or defined, often introducing a reason or clarification: "the thing about ~ is..." / "what I mean by ~ is...".

examples.japanese: 彼が会社を辞めたというのは、本当ですか。
examples.english: Is it true, this thing about him quitting the company?

examples.japanese: 一人暮らしというのは、自由な反面、寂しいものだ。
examples.english: Living alone, you see, is lonely, even though it's also free.

matcher: って
explanation: Casual spoken contraction that can mark a quotation (like と言った) or a topic (like は), depending on context: "he said ~" / "as for ~".

examples.japanese: 田中さん、来月結婚するんだって。
examples.english: I heard Tanaka-san is getting married next month.

examples.japanese: カレーって、辛ければ辛いほどおいしいよね。
examples.english: Curry, you know, is tastier the spicier it is.

matcher: ことにします|ことにした|ことにする|ことにしている|ことにしました
explanation: Attaches to a verb's dictionary or negative form to state the speaker's own decision: "I've decided to ~", as opposed to ことになる's decision made by circumstance or another party.

examples.japanese: 来年、大学院に進むことにしました。
examples.english: I've decided to go on to graduate school next year.

examples.japanese: 健康のために、毎朝走ることにしている。
examples.english: For my health, I've made it a habit to run every morning.

matcher: ことになります|ことになった|ことになる|ことになっている|ことになりました
explanation: Attaches to a verb's dictionary or negative form to describe an arrangement or result decided by circumstance, convention, or someone else, not the speaker: "it has been decided that ~" / "it turns out that ~".

examples.japanese: 来月から大阪支社で働くことになりました。
examples.english: It's been decided that I'll work at the Osaka branch starting next month.

examples.japanese: 会議は来週の月曜日に行われることになっている。
examples.english: It's set that the meeting will be held next Monday.

matcher: 抜きます|抜いた|抜く|抜いて
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to mean carrying an effortful action all the way through to the end, often under difficulty: "~ through to the end" / "manage to fully ~".

examples.japanese: 苦しいマラソンを最後まで走り抜いた。
examples.english: I ran the grueling marathon all the way through to the end.

examples.japanese: どんなに辛くても、この試練を生き抜きます。
examples.english: No matter how hard it is, I will survive through this ordeal.

matcher: きります|きった|きれない|きって|きれません
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to mean completing an action fully or using something up entirely: "finish ~ing completely" / "~ all the way", and in negative form "can't fully ~".

examples.japanese: この本は面白くて、一日で読みきってしまった。
examples.english: This book was so interesting that I finished reading it completely in one day.

examples.japanese: こんなに量が多いと、一人では食べきれない。
examples.english: With this much food, I can't eat it all by myself.

matcher: がちだ|がちです|がちな|がちの
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem or noun to describe a tendency toward something usually undesirable happening often: "tends to ~" / "prone to ~".

examples.japanese: 一人暮らしを始めてから、食事がおろそかになりがちだ。
examples.english: Since starting to live alone, I've tended to neglect my meals.

examples.japanese: 冬は日照時間が短く、風邪をひきがちな季節です。
examples.english: Winter is a season with short daylight hours, one where people tend to catch colds.

matcher: っぽいです|っぽかった|っぽい
explanation: Attaches to a noun or verb's stem to describe a strong impression of that quality, often with a slightly negative or casual nuance: "~ish" / "seems very ~".

examples.japanese: 彼はもう30歳なのに、まだ子供っぽいところがある。
examples.english: Even though he's already 30, he still has a childish side.

examples.japanese: あの人の話し方は、なんだか嘘っぽかった。
examples.english: That person's way of talking somehow seemed fishy, like a lie.

matcher: 代わりに
explanation: Attaches to a noun or plain-form clause to mark a substitution or a balancing trade-off: "instead of ~" / "in exchange for ~, ...".

examples.japanese: 今日は父の代わりに、私が会議に出席します。
examples.english: Today, I'll attend the meeting in place of my father.

examples.japanese: このアプリは無料である代わりに、広告が多い。
examples.english: In exchange for this app being free, it has a lot of ads.

matcher: おかげで|おかげだ|おかげです
explanation: Attaches to a noun or plain-form clause to credit a positive result to its cause: "thanks to ~" / "because of ~ (which helped)".

examples.japanese: 先生が丁寧に教えてくれたおかげで、試験に合格できた。
examples.english: Thanks to the teacher explaining things carefully, I was able to pass the exam.

examples.japanese: 皆さんのご協力のおかげです。本当にありがとうございました。
examples.english: It's thanks to everyone's cooperation. Thank you so much.

matcher: せいで|せいだ|せいです|せいにする
explanation: Attaches to a noun or plain-form clause to blame a negative result on its cause: "because of ~ (which caused the problem)" -- the negative counterpart of おかげで.

examples.japanese: 昨日夜更かししたせいで、今日は頭が痛い。
examples.english: Because I stayed up late last night, my head hurts today.

examples.japanese: 失敗を人のせいにするのはよくない。
examples.english: It's not good to blame your failures on other people.

matcher: ふりをする|ふりをした|ふりをして|ふりをしている
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form clause or noun+の to describe putting on an act: "pretend to ~" / "act as if ~".

examples.japanese: 授業中、眠いのに起きているふりをした。
examples.english: During class, even though I was sleepy, I pretended to be awake.

examples.japanese: 彼女は聞こえないふりをして、返事をしなかった。
examples.english: She pretended not to hear and didn't respond.

matcher: せられる|せられた|せられます|せられて
explanation: Combines the causative (make/let someone do) with the passive, describing being forced into doing something against one's will: "be made to ~" / "be forced to ~".

examples.japanese: 子供の頃、嫌いな野菜を毎回食べさせられた。
examples.english: As a child, I was made to eat vegetables I disliked every time.

examples.japanese: 上司の話が長くて、一時間も待たせられた。
examples.english: My boss's talk went on so long that I was made to wait a whole hour.

matcher: ことなく
explanation: Attaches to a verb's dictionary form to mean an expected action never happened: "without ever ~ing", a slightly literary equivalent of ～ないで.

examples.japanese: 彼は一度も諦めることなく、最後まで挑戦し続けた。
examples.english: He kept challenging himself to the very end, without ever giving up even once.

examples.japanese: そのニュースは誰にも知られることなく、ひっそりと消えていった。
examples.english: The news quietly faded away without anyone ever finding out.

matcher: ままだ|ままです|まま|ままで
explanation: Attaches to a verb's た-form, ない-form, or a noun+の, describing a state that continues unchanged while something else happens: "as is" / "while still ~ing/being ~".

examples.japanese: 電気をつけたまま、寝てしまった。
examples.english: I fell asleep with the light left on.

examples.japanese: 靴を履いたままの姿で家に上がってしまった。
examples.english: I ended up going up into the house still wearing my shoes.

matcher: きり
explanation: Attaches to a verb's た-form or a noun to mark that nothing has happened since that one occasion: "ever since ~" / "only that once and then nothing more".

examples.japanese: 彼とは去年の同窓会で会ったきりだ。
examples.english: I haven't seen him since we met at last year's reunion.

examples.japanese: 祖母は入院してから、寝たきりの生活を送っている。
examples.english: Since being hospitalized, my grandmother has been living bedridden.

matcher: つつあります|つつあった|つつある
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to describe a change that is gradually, currently underway: "is in the process of ~ing", a formal-sounding alternative to ～ている for ongoing change.

examples.japanese: 地球の気温は年々上昇しつつある。
examples.english: The Earth's temperature is gradually rising year by year.

examples.japanese: この町の人口は少しずつ減りつつあります。
examples.english: This town's population is gradually decreasing little by little.

matcher: つつも|つつ
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to link two actions happening at once, or -- especially with も -- to admit a contradiction: "while ~ing" / "even though ~".

examples.japanese: 体に悪いと知りつつ、たばこをやめられない。
examples.english: Even though I know it's bad for my body, I can't quit smoking.

examples.japanese: 忙しいと言いつつも、彼は毎週映画を見に行っている。
examples.english: Even while saying he's busy, he goes to see a movie every week.

matcher: ばよかった|ればよかった|なければよかった
explanation: Attaches to a verb's ば-conditional form to express regret over something not done (or, in negative, something done): "I wish I had ~" / "I should have ~".

examples.japanese: もっと早く相談すればよかった。
examples.english: I wish I had consulted someone sooner.

examples.japanese: あんなことを言わなければよかった。
examples.english: I wish I hadn't said something like that.

matcher: あげくに|あげく
explanation: Attaches to a verb's た-form or noun+の, marking the (usually bad) final result after a long process of trouble: "after all that ~, in the end...".

examples.japanese: 何時間も悩んだあげく、結局買わないことにした。
examples.english: After agonizing over it for hours, in the end I decided not to buy it.

examples.japanese: さんざん道に迷ったあげくに、約束の時間に遅れてしまった。
examples.english: After getting hopelessly lost, in the end I was late for the appointment.

matcher: 一方で|一方
explanation: Attaches to a clause to contrast it with another fact about the same subject happening at the same time: "while, on the other hand, ~" / "even as ~".

examples.japanese: この薬は効果が高い一方で、副作用も強い。
examples.english: While this medicine is highly effective, it also has strong side effects.

examples.japanese: 都市の人口が増える一方、地方の人口は減り続けている。
examples.english: Even as city populations grow, rural populations keep decreasing.

matcher: うちに
explanation: Attaches to a verb's plain form or adjective to mark a window of opportunity before a state changes: "while ~ (before it's too late)" / "before ~ changes".

examples.japanese: 温かいうちに、このスープを飲んでください。
examples.english: Please drink this soup while it's still warm.

examples.japanese: 子供が小さいうちに、家族でたくさん旅行しておきたい。
examples.english: While the kids are still small, I want to travel a lot as a family.

matcher: おそれがある|おそれがあります|おそれがあった
explanation: Attaches to a verb's dictionary form or noun+の, formally warning of a negative possibility: "there is a risk/danger that ~".

examples.japanese: 大雨のため、川が氾濫するおそれがあります。
examples.english: Due to heavy rain, there is a risk that the river will flood.

examples.japanese: この薬には副作用が出るおそれがある。
examples.english: This medicine carries a risk of side effects appearing.

matcher: かけの|かけて|かけだ|かけです
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to describe an action left partway done, not yet finished: "half-~ed" / "in the middle of ~ing when interrupted".

examples.japanese: テーブルの上に食べかけのケーキが置いてある。
examples.english: There's a half-eaten cake sitting on the table.

examples.japanese: 何か言いかけて、彼は口をつぐんだ。
examples.english: He started to say something, then fell silent.

matcher: がたいです|がたかった|がたい
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to mean an action is emotionally or practically very difficult to do: "hard to ~" / "can hardly bring oneself to ~", stronger and more formal than ～にくい.

examples.japanese: 彼が犯人だとは、どうしても信じがたい。
examples.english: I find it hard to believe, no matter what, that he's the culprit.

examples.japanese: あの日の光景は今でも忘れがたい。
examples.english: The scene from that day is still hard to forget, even now.

matcher: かどうか
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form clause to embed a yes/no question inside a larger sentence: "whether or not ~".

examples.japanese: この計画がうまくいくかどうか、まだわからない。
examples.english: I still don't know whether this plan will go well or not.

examples.japanese: 彼が本当のことを言っているかどうか、確かめてみよう。
examples.english: Let's check whether or not he's telling the truth.

matcher: からすると|からすれば|からいうと|から見ると
explanation: Attaches to a noun to frame a judgment from a particular standpoint: "judging from ~" / "from the perspective of ~".

examples.japanese: あの雲の様子からすると、もうすぐ雨が降りそうだ。
examples.english: Judging from the look of those clouds, it seems it'll rain soon.

examples.japanese: 専門家の立場からいうと、この計画には無理がある。
examples.english: From an expert's standpoint, this plan is unreasonable.

matcher: からには
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form clause to mean that, given this fact is true, a certain obligation or determination naturally follows: "now that ~" / "since ~, one must...".

examples.japanese: 引き受けたからには、最後まで責任を持ってやります。
examples.english: Now that I've taken it on, I'll see it through responsibly to the end.

examples.japanese: 日本に住むからには、日本語をきちんと勉強したい。
examples.english: Since I'm going to live in Japan, I want to study Japanese properly.

matcher: くせに
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form clause, adjective, or noun+の to point out a contradiction with a critical or mocking tone: "even though ~ (which makes this worse)".

examples.japanese: 自分は遅刻したくせに、私を叱った。
examples.english: Even though he was the one who was late, he scolded me.

examples.japanese: 何も知らないくせに、偉そうなことを言うな。
examples.english: Don't talk so high and mighty when you don't even know anything.

matcher: さえすれば|さえあれば|さえ.*ば
explanation: Combines さえ ("even/just") with a ば-conditional to isolate the one necessary condition for something: "as long as ~" / "if only ~, that's all it takes".

examples.japanese: お金さえあれば、幸せになれるわけではない。
examples.english: It's not that you can become happy just because you have money.

examples.japanese: あなたが謝りさえすれば、彼はきっと許してくれる。
examples.english: As long as you just apologize, he'll surely forgive you.

matcher: 次第|次第だ|次第です
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem to mean "as soon as ~" (immediately following), or to a noun to mean a result "depends entirely on ~".

examples.japanese: 空港に着き次第、ご連絡いたします。
examples.english: I'll contact you as soon as I arrive at the airport.

examples.japanese: 参加できるかどうかは、天気次第だ。
examples.english: Whether or not we can participate depends entirely on the weather.

matcher: たびに
explanation: Attaches to a verb's dictionary form or noun+の to mean that something happens every single time a certain event occurs: "every time ~" / "whenever ~".

examples.japanese: この曲を聞くたびに、学生時代を思い出す。
examples.english: Every time I hear this song, I remember my student days.

examples.japanese: 旅行のたびに、その土地の名物を食べるようにしている。
examples.english: Every time I travel, I make a point of eating that region's local specialty.

matcher: だけあって|だけあり|だけのことはある
explanation: Attaches to a noun or plain-form clause praising a fitting result given some background: "as one would expect from ~" / "given that ~, no wonder...".

examples.japanese: さすが一流ホテルだけあって、サービスが素晴らしい。
examples.english: As you'd expect from a first-class hotel, the service is wonderful.

examples.japanese: 彼女は10年間ピアノを習っていただけあって、演奏が本当に美しい。
examples.english: Given that she's studied piano for ten years, her playing is truly beautiful.

matcher: だけに
explanation: Attaches to a noun or plain-form clause to mean that, precisely because of this fact, the result is even more pronounced than usual: "precisely because ~" / "all the more so since ~".

examples.japanese: 期待していただけに、試験に落ちたショックは大きかった。
examples.english: Precisely because I had my hopes up, the shock of failing the exam was huge.

examples.japanese: 有名な選手だけに、彼のミスは大きく報道された。
examples.english: Precisely because he's a famous athlete, his mistake was widely reported.

matcher: てからでないと|てからでなければ
explanation: Attaches to a verb's て-form to mean a following action is impossible until the first one is completed: "not until after ~" / "unless ~ first, ... can't happen".

examples.japanese: 医者に相談してからでないと、薬は飲めません。
examples.english: I can't take the medicine until I've consulted a doctor first.

examples.japanese: 実物を見てからでなければ、値段は決められない。
examples.english: I can't decide on a price unless I see the actual item first.

matcher: てたまらない|でたまらない
explanation: Attaches to an adjective's or emotion-verb's て-form to express an intense, hard-to-control feeling: "unbearably ~" / "can't stand how ~".

examples.japanese: 引っ越したばかりで、友達に会いたくてたまらない。
examples.english: I just moved, and I miss my friends unbearably.

examples.japanese: 一日中歩き回って、足が痛くてたまらない。
examples.english: I walked around all day, and my legs hurt unbearably.

matcher: てならない|でならない
explanation: Attaches to an emotion adjective's or verb's て-form to express a feeling that wells up naturally and can't be suppressed: "can't help ~ing" / "irresistibly feel ~".

examples.japanese: 一人で暮らす祖母のことが心配でならない。
examples.english: I can't help worrying about my grandmother who lives alone.

examples.japanese: なぜか、あの映画の結末が気になってならない。
examples.english: For some reason, I can't stop thinking about that movie's ending.

matcher: ということだ|ということです|とのことだ|とのことです
explanation: Attaches to a plain-form clause to report information heard from another source, or to restate/clarify a meaning: "I hear that ~" / "that means ~".

examples.japanese: 天気予報によると、明日は台風が来るということだ。
examples.english: According to the weather forecast, I hear a typhoon is coming tomorrow.

examples.japanese: 社長は来月退職するとのことです。
examples.english: I've been told that the president will retire next month.

matcher: というより
explanation: Attaches to a noun or plain-form clause to reject one description in favor of a more accurate one: "rather than say ~, it's more like ...".

examples.japanese: 彼は厳しいというより、真面目なだけだと思う。
examples.english: Rather than saying he's strict, I think he's just serious.

examples.japanese: これは失敗というより、新しい発見だったと言える。
examples.english: Rather than calling this a failure, you could say it was a new discovery.

matcher: とおりに|どおりに|とおりだ|どおりだ|通りに
explanation: Attaches to a verb's dictionary/past form or noun+の, marking that something matches exactly: "just as ~" / "in accordance with ~".

examples.japanese: 先生に教わったとおりに、丁寧に手順を進めた。
examples.english: I carefully carried out the steps, just as the teacher had taught me.

examples.japanese: 計画どおりに、プロジェクトは無事終わった。
examples.english: In accordance with the plan, the project finished safely.

matcher: ないことには
explanation: Attaches to a verb's negative form to mean that, without that first condition being met, nothing further can happen: "unless ~ (first), ... won't happen".

examples.japanese: 実際にやってみないことには、成功するかどうかわからない。
examples.english: Unless I actually try it, I won't know whether it'll succeed.

examples.japanese: お金を払わないことには、この商品は受け取れない。
examples.english: Unless you pay, you can't receive this product.

matcher: ないことはない|ないこともない
explanation: Attaches to a verb's negative form as a double negative, cautiously admitting a possibility: "it's not that ~ isn't possible" / "I suppose ~ could happen".

examples.japanese: 頑張れば、締め切りに間に合わないことはない。
examples.english: If I work hard, it's not impossible to make the deadline.

examples.japanese: 忙しいけど、少しなら手伝えないこともない。
examples.english: I'm busy, but I suppose I could help a little.

matcher: ながらも|ながら
explanation: Attaches to a verb's stem or adjective to admit a contradiction between two facts about the same subject: "even though ~" / "while ~, nonetheless...", a more literary concessive than けど.

examples.japanese: 狭いながらも、居心地のいい部屋に住んでいる。
examples.english: Even though it's small, I live in a cozy, comfortable room.

examples.japanese: 彼は忙しいと知りながら、頼み事をしてしまった。
examples.english: Even though I knew he was busy, I ended up asking him a favor.

matcher: において|における|に於いて
explanation: A formal equivalent of で/に marking the place, time, or field something occurs in: "in ~" / "at ~", common in written and official Japanese.

examples.japanese: 本日の式典は大ホールにおいて行われます。
examples.english: Today's ceremony will be held in the main hall.

examples.japanese: 現代社会における教育の役割は大きい。
examples.english: The role of education in modern society is significant.

matcher: にかかわらず|にもかかわらず
explanation: Attaches to a noun or pair of opposites, meaning a result holds no matter which condition applies: "regardless of ~" / "whether or not ~".

examples.japanese: 天気にかかわらず、運動会は予定どおり行われます。
examples.english: Regardless of the weather, the sports day will be held as scheduled.

examples.japanese: 何度も注意したにもかかわらず、彼は同じ間違いを繰り返した。
examples.english: Despite being warned many times, he repeated the same mistake.

matcher: に決まっている|に決まっています|に決まってる
